question: Which statement best describes Main idea?
options: `<` displays the less-than sign `<`. Without the reference, the browser may treat a following word as the start of an HTML tag. It is like quoting a symbol so it is read aloud instead of treated as an instruction. This is especially useful when teaching HTML or showing code examples. For example, write `<button>` when showing an opening tag as visible text.

Modern HTML documents usually use UTF-8, which can represent a wide range of characters directly. You do not need to memorize a reference for every accented letter or symbol. It is like using a keyboard that supports the character rather than looking up a code. Ensure the document declares the correct encoding. For example, insert user-provided strings as text instead of building an HTML fragment.

`&` displays an ampersand `&`. The ampersand also begins many character references, so writing it directly in some attribute values can make the text ambiguous. It is like a punctuation mark that also starts a special instruction. Escape it when needed, especially in URLs and hand-written markup. For example, escape an ampersand in a URL when it separates query parameters in HTML markup.

`>` displays the greater-than sign `>`. Together, `<` and `>` can show angle brackets around a tag name as visible text. They work like quotation marks around a symbol. When displaying user-provided content, use safe text APIs and established escaping instead of building HTML strings by hand. For example, use UTF-8 for ordinary language characters rather than memorizing many numeric references.
explanation: `<` displays the less-than sign `<`. Without the reference, the browser may treat a following word as the start of an HTML tag. It is like quoting a symbol so it is read aloud instead of treated as an instruction. This is especially useful when teaching HTML or showing code examples. For example, write `<button>` when showing an opening tag as visible text.
